content_metadata.description: This video explains the concept of fictitious forces and their applications in real-world scenarios. It features a stick figure, Mario, illustrated in different non-inertial frames to demonstrate various fictitious forces such as translational, centrifugal, Coriolis, and Euler forces.

qAndA.question: What direction does the force push you when you are in an elevator going down?

qAndA.answer: Because it is caused by the car's deceleration, making your frame of reference non-inertial. The actual force acting on you is your inertia trying to keep you moving at the original speed.
qAndA.question: In the car crash scenario, why is the force throwing you forward fictitious?
What mathematical operation is involved in calculating the Coriolis force?
In the Euler force scenario, what changes in the merry-go-round's motion?

qAndA.answer: The video starts with a neutral and informative mood, gradually building curiosity and then transitions to a more cautionary mood in the car crash scene. The ending is a blend of neutral and thought-provoking.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood of the video?

Arrows indicate the direction of acceleration and force
Formula: 'a=d²R/dt²' (acceleration) is shown

The narrator explains the centrifugal force

Formula: 'F(centrifugal) = -F(centripetal)' is shown

Formula: '|F(centrifugal)| = mω²r' is shown

The narrator explains the Coriolis force

activities.description: Mario is standing on a merry-go-round that's being pushed, causing a change in angular velocity
The narrator explains the Euler force

Arrows indicate the direction of angular velocity (ω), the change in angular velocity (dΩ/dt), and the Euler force
Formula: 'F(euler) = -m (dΩ/dt) x r' is shown

activities.description: The narrator summarizes the concept of fictitious forces and their application in non-inertial frames
A car crash scenario is presented to demonstrate the real-world implications of fictitious forces

narrativeProgression.description: Summarizes that all real and fictitious forces must be considered in non-inertial frames to determine acceleration using Newton's Second Law
Uses a car crash scenario to demonstrate that while the feeling of being thrown forward during deceleration is a fictitious force, the impact is real. Emphasizes the importance of seatbelts

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Consider taking off on an airplane, now riding a merry-go-round.
And finally, going down and lift.
On the airplane, we'll fill us if you're being pushed backwards into your seat.
On a merry-go-round, you'd fill us if you're being pushed outwards.
On the lifts, you'd fill us if you're floating.
Now what do all these events have in common?
Well, it turns out that all these forces pushing us up, down or outwards are actually not real.
They only appear to act on objects, or in this case us.
We call them Fixitious Forces.
A Fixitious Force is an apparent force that acts upon all masses whose motion is described
using a non-inertial frame of reference.
An inertial frame is one where there is direct acceleration, so either remain stationary
or move that constant velocity.
Newton's laws of motion apply, for example an airport.
A non-inertial reference frame moves in a non-uniform or accelerated motion,
so when the plane leaves the runway, it is accelerating, so it is a non-inertial reference frame.
Here Newton's laws of motion do not apply.
Fixitious forces are introduced so that Newton's second law is valid in a non-inertial frame.
Imagine that Mario is standing on a plane, which is taking off with an acceleration A.
He feels the force pushing him backwards.
Due to the reference frame's motion, it appears that Mario is being pushed in the direction opposite
to acceleration of the plane.
This is called the Translation of Fixitious Force.
The second Fixitious Force is called the centrifugal force.
Imagine Mario is standing on a merry-go-round, which is spinning with an angular velocity omega.
To an inertial observer on the ground, it is easy to see that to keep Mario in his rotational motion,
a continuous centripetal force must be applied perpendicular to his direction of motion.
This is equal to M v squared over R.
This force will be pushing Mario radially inwards.
Now, from Mario's point of view of the rotating non-inertial frame,
he feels an apparent force pushing him outwards.
This is called the centrifugal force, and will be equal in modulus and opposite in direction
with respect to the centripetal force.
We also know that the velocity v is equal to the angular velocity omega multiplied by the radius,
so we can rewrite the centrifugal force as M R omega squared.
To explain the cruelest force, we first need to introduce a new vector.
So imagine a merry-go-round, this spinning with an angular velocity omega.
We introduce a vector perpendicular to the plane of rotation,
represented by a capital omega, called angular velocity vector.
Imagine Mario is running across the merry-go-round with a velocity v.
There will be a fictitious force, the cruelest force acting on him,
which is given by an active M times v cross omega.
We'll need to use the right hand rule because of the cross-product.
The next tip sign in the equation means that the cruelest force is pointing in the opposite direction.
So in this case, the cruelest force will be pointing inwards.
The last fictitious force is called the u-the-force or as a muthophores.
Imagine Mario is standing on the merry-go-round with a distance R from the center,
and someone is pushing him.
This will cause a change in angular velocity.
We can express this as a vector d omega dt.
The fictitious u-the-force acting on him is given by negative M d omega dt cross R.
In this case, the cross-product will give vector-cushing Mario inwards.
If a person in an accelerating non-inertial reference string
wanted to find their acceleration,
then we need to add up all the real and fictitious forces together.
This is the form that Newton's second law takes in non-inertial frames.
Fictitious forces are present in our everyday lives.
We've just grown so used to them that we've very noticed them anymore.
Now remember, the pseudo-force that is felt during acceleration
can also be felt during deceleration only in the other direction.
So next time you get in a car, put on your seatbelt.
The force from your forward during crash might be fictitious,
but the impact will be real.

youtube_description:
Fictitious Forces can often be confusing. Why do we use them if they are just apparent forces? In which cases do we use each force? 
This video by UCL Physics Students will try to explain with simple but effective examples what each fictitious force represents and why they are so useful in describing non-inertial frames.
